data.Documented value: Tempering Bankruptcy Nondischargability to Promote the Purposes of Student Loans

Student loans, unlike other debts, are not dischargeable in bankruptcy unless the debtor starts a special proceeding and proves that repayment would cause “undue hardship.” This requirement probably accounts for the fact that only a tiny fraction of bankrupt debtors succeed in discharging their student loans. This article is the first to make the case that student- loan nondischargeability interferes with achieving the student-loan pro- grams’ goals and to propose solutions that courts and the Department of Education (the Department) can employ under current law. The article draws on the legislative history of the student-loan programs to establish that they serve at least four distinct purposes: providing equality of access to higher education, educating the population for the benefit of the country, enabling students’ free choice of career, and providing a bene- fit to students. The article then looks to the empirical literature and to fundamental precepts of bankruptcy law to show that nondischargeability can thwart the purposes of the student-loan programs through four different effects: deter- ring students from higher education, distorting career choice, discouraging borrowers from economic and social participation, and rendering student loans harmful to borrowers. Accordingly, nondischargeability should be applied narrowly, only in situations where its goals are advanced without undue interference with other goals of the programs. The article offers ideas for tempering each of the four negative effects. To avoid deterring education, the fact that bankruptcy relief often can be had if requested should be made more salient. To combat distortion of career choice, bankruptcy courts should stop ruling that debtors should abandon lower-paying jobs for which their education has prepared them. To mitigate borrower discouragement and harm, courts and the Department should take account of the likelihood of these effects in deciding on discharge. The debt-income ratio may be a proxy for discouragement, and inability to find a job in one’s field may be a proxy for harm.

The Seventeenth Annual Emory Bankruptcy Developments Journal Symposium This Paper presumes that readers want to make bankruptcy more useful for consumers and for society as a whole. If this is true, we need to ask two questions: first, what do individual consumers hope to get out of the system, and second, what does society hope to get out of the system? Part I of this Paper discusses the increase in debt over the last two decades, the growing wage and income gap, growing debt inequality and race, and the fall of the CFPB, all justifications for using the bankruptcy system to help ameliorate these problems. Part II discusses particular ways the Code could be amended to become more relevant, including allowing all secured debt to be stripped down and allowing more student loans to be discharged. Part III discusses the main policy justifications for our consumer bankruptcy system and suggests a third system modification that would make bankruptcy more relevant for consumers, namely a hearing or other forum in which consumers could be publicly forgiven of their debts and perhaps even be heard about their financial woes through the bankruptcy court system.

sections.heading: Tempering Bankruptcy Nondischargability to Promote the Purposes of Student Loans

The article, authored by scholars at Southern Methodist University Law Review, contends that the requirement that student loans be discharged only under specific conditions and procedures is a significant barrier to achieving the goals of student loans, which include promoting equality of access to higher education, educating the population for the benefit of the country, enabling students' free choice of career, and providing a benefit to students. [[S2|SMU Law Review]] The article draws on the legislative history of the student-loan programs to establish that they serve at least four distinct purposes: providing equality of access to higher education, educating the population for the benefit of the country, enabling students' free choice of career, and providing a benefit to students. It then examines the empirical literature and fundamental principles of bankruptcy law to demonstrate that nondischargeability can thwart these purposes through four different effects: deterring students from higher education, distorting career choice, discouraging borrowers from economic and social participation, and rendering student loans harmful to borrowers.

[[S2|SMU Law Review]] The article proposes that nondischargeability should be applied narrowly, only in situations where its goals are advanced without undue interference with other goals of the programs. It suggests ideas for tempering each of the four negative effects. To avoid deterring education, the article recommends that the fact that bankruptcy relief often can be had if requested should be made more salient. To combat distortion of career choice, bankruptcy courts should stop ruling that debtors should abandon lower-paying jobs for which their education has prepared them.

To mitigate borrower discouragement and harm, courts and the Department of Education should take account of the likelihood of these effects in deciding on discharge. sections.heading: Bringing Relevance Back to Consumer Bankruptcy
paragraphs: In the realm of consumer bankruptcy, there is a growing recognition that the system can indeed be made more relevant to the needs of consumers and society as a whole. This paper, presented at the University of New Mexico’s Digital Repository, underscores the importance of understanding what individual consumers and society as a whole hope to achieve through the bankruptcy process. [[S3|UNM’s Digital Repository University of New]] The first question to consider is what individual consumers hope to get out of the system. Traditionally, bankruptcy has been viewed as a last resort for those who cannot pay their debts.

However, the paper suggests that consumers may have different expectations. For instance, they might hope to avoid the stigma of bankruptcy, to regain control over their finances, or to clear their credit history. Additionally, consumers might want to use bankruptcy as a tool to protect their assets or to negotiate better terms with creditors. [[S3|UNM’s Digital Repository University of New]] The second question to consider is what society hopes to get out of the system.

The paper argues that the current system is not serving its intended purpose. It suggests that the growing debt inequality, the widening wage and income gap, and the decline of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) have led to a system that is not addressing these issues effectively. The CFPB, which was supposed to protect consumers from financial abuse, has been weakened, leaving consumers without the necessary tools to navigate the complex world of debt. [[S3|UNM’s Digital Repository University of New]] To make the system more relevant, the paper proposes several amendments to the Code.

One of the main suggestions is to allow all secured debt to be stripped down. This would simplify the bankruptcy process for consumers and make it more accessible. Another amendment is to allow more student loans to be discharged. This would help alleviate the burden of student debt, which is a significant issue for many borrowers.

[[S3|UNM’s Digital Repository University of New]] [[S3|UNM’s Digital Repository University of New]] The paper also discusses the main policy justifications for our consumer bankruptcy system. It suggests that a third system modification would make bankruptcy more relevant for consumers. This modification would involve a hearing or other forum where consumers could be publicly forgiven of their debts. This would provide a platform for consumers to share their financial struggles and receive support, which could help rebuild their credit and regain control over their finances.

sections.heading: Lawmakers Want to Lower Student Loan Interest Rates. Experts Say
paragraphs: Lawmakers Want to Lower Student Loan Interest Rates. Experts Say There Are Better Ways to Help Borrowers [[S7|U S News Money]] The U.S. News - Money article highlights that lawmakers are actively seeking to reduce the interest rates on student loans. This initiative comes as a response to the growing concerns about the high cost of student debt, which has become a significant burden for many borrowers.

The experts involved in this debate emphasize that while lowering interest rates is a crucial step, it is not the only solution to address the issue of student loan debt. [[S7|U S News Money]] One of the key points made by the experts is that there are alternative methods that can help borrowers manage their student loan payments more effectively. For instance, the article mentions that some experts suggest exploring income-driven repayment plans, which adjust the monthly payment based on the borrower's income. This can significantly reduce the financial strain on borrowers who are struggling to make payments while still allowing them to pay off their loans over time.

[[S7|U S News Money]] Another suggestion is to explore forgiveness programs, where borrowers can apply for a reduction or complete their loans through a combination of income-driven payments and other repayment options. This approach can provide relief to those who are unable to make payments due to financial difficulties but still want to avoid the full repayment of their loans. [[S7|U S News Money]] The experts also argue that focusing solely on lowering interest rates may not be the most effective solution. They point out that the high cost of student loans is often due to the complexity of the repayment process and the lack of clear information for borrowers.

By simplifying the repayment process and providing more transparency, experts believe that borrowers can better manage their finances and avoid the stress of high interest rates. [[S7|U S News Money]] The experts also suggest that policymakers should consider the long-term impact of student loan debt on the economy. They argue that by providing better support and guidance to borrowers, policymakers can help prevent the negative effects of student loan debt on future generations. This includes providing resources for borrowers to understand their options and making it easier for them to navigate the complex repayment process.
